mcqs.question: A function parameter is declared as type String (not String?). What does Kotlin's compiler guarantee about it?
options: Nothing extra — it behaves identically to a nullable type at runtime
It only affects IDE warnings, not actual compilation
The value is guaranteed non-null only in debug builds
The compiler guarantees the value can never be null at that point, and refuses to compile code that would pass a nullable value there without an explicit null check or assertion
mcqs.explanation: A non-nullable type is a compile-time guarantee enforced by the type system — passing a nullable value where a non-nullable type is expected fails to compile unless explicitly handled (a null check, ?:, or !!), which is the core mechanism that eliminates the class of NullPointerExceptions common in pre-null-safety Java Android code.

mcqs.question: A sealed class UiState has three subtypes, and a when block handles all three with no else branch. A new subtype UiState.Empty is added later. What happens to that existing when block?
options: It continues to compile and simply never matches the new Empty case at runtime
It fails to compile, since the when is no longer exhaustive over the sealed class's now-larger set of subtypes — this is the compiler protection sealed classes specifically provide
It automatically falls through to a default no-op branch
Sealed classes don't support adding new subtypes after the fact at all
mcqs.explanation: Because the compiler tracks the complete, closed set of a sealed class's subtypes, adding a new one makes any exhaustive when missing a branch for it a compile error, not a silently-skipped runtime case — this is exactly the safety guarantee sealed classes provide over an open hierarchy or enum.

mcqs.question: Why are extension functions especially useful for adding helper behavior to Android framework classes like View?
options: Framework classes automatically detect and merge extension function behavior into their own methods
Extension functions require modifying the framework class's source code

Extension functions let you add method-call-syntax behavior to a type you don't own and often can't subclass (many framework classes are final or otherwise impractical to extend), without wrapper classes or awkward static utility calls
Extension functions are only usable within the same module as the class they extend
mcqs.explanation: Extension functions add convenience behavior onto any existing type, including ones you don't own and can't subclass, resolving at compile time to a regular function call while reading exactly like a real member call — this is precisely why they're the idiomatic fit for adding helpers onto Android framework types like View or Context.

mcqs.question: A developer wants to configure several properties on a newly created object and then have the expression return that same object for further chaining. Which scope function fits?
options: let, since it's the most commonly used scope function
apply, since it returns the original object itself (accessed as this inside the block) after running the configuration block
run, since it always returns the original receiver
with, since it's designed specifically for object construction
mcqs.explanation: apply is specifically designed for configuring an object's properties and then returning that same object, making it the standard fit for builder-style chains — run and let return the lambda's result rather than the original object, and with is meant for grouping calls on an object that already exists, not construction chaining.

mcqs.question: A codebase uses !! at nearly every point a nullable value appears, reasoning that the types are all still correctly nullable-annotated. What's the flaw in that reasoning?
options: There's no flaw — as long as types are correctly annotated as nullable, using !! everywhere is equally safe
!! is deprecated and will be removed in future Kotlin versions

Each !! is a deliberate opt-out of compile-time safety, checked at runtime instead — if the assertion is ever wrong, it crashes with the exact same NullPointerException null safety was designed to prevent, just at a line the compiler had already flagged as risky
!! only affects performance, not correctness
mcqs.explanation: Correctly annotating nullable types doesn't help if every actual use immediately asserts non-null with !! — that reverses the safety by deferring the check to runtime, reproducing the exact crash class null safety exists to eliminate, just with the compiler having already flagged the risk at that specific line.

mcqs.question: A developer defines an extension function with the same name and signature as an existing member function on the same type, intending it to override the member's behavior. What actually happens when it's called?
options: The extension function runs first, then falls back to the member function
The extension function successfully overrides the member as intended, since extensions take priority by default
This causes a compile-time ambiguity error requiring the developer to rename one of them

Kotlin's resolution always prefers the member function over an extension with the same signature, so the extension is silently never called through normal dispatch — with no compiler error or warning pointing at the problem
mcqs.explanation: Kotlin always resolves to the member function when a member and an extension share the same name and signature, silently — the extension isn't an error, it's just never invoked through that call path, which is exactly why intending an extension to override member behavior doesn't work; genuine overriding requires real inheritance, not a statically-resolved extension function.
